claims.text: HTTP/3 requires materially more CPU time and memory than HTTP/2 per connection, making it costlier to operate at scale. This cost difference is significant enough that companies optimizing for engagement (Google, Akamai) treat it as an explicit tradeoff—they deploy HTTP/3 because engagement gains offset the infrastructure expense. For operators running less performance-sensitive workloads, this cost-benefit calculation may not favor HTTP/3.

claims.text: Mid-band NR-SA's latency advantage derives from two independent sources: the lower signaling overhead inherent to SA architecture, and denser mid-band deployment. T-Mobile's n41 (SA) was deployed with 462 unique cell-site PCIs, compared to AT&T and Verizon NSA mid-band channels with substantially lower PCI counts (AT&T n77: 152; Verizon n77: 147), representing a 3x density differential. This means NSA-only operators can partially reduce latency disadvantage relative to SA competitors through matching deployment density, but remain constrained by NSA's architecturally inherent signaling overhead regardless of deployment depth.
